verdicts.quote: An attacker can craft an AMQP message with a length-prefixed field claiming up to 2.1GB of data. The client will attempt to allocate a 2.1GB byte array, causing OutOfMemoryError and denial of service.
verdicts.why: F04 is exactly about the attacker-controlled length prefix driving the allocation size. Its evidence shows `final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt());` followed by `final byte [] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength];` and only then `in.readFully(buffer);` — the array is sized from untrusted input and created before the payload is known to exist. That is the mechanism D1 describes, and it is what F04 says is exploitable (OOM DoS), not an incidental mention.

verdicts.quote: An attacker can craft an AMQP message containing tables nested 10,000+ levels deep. Each level consumes stack frame space. This causes StackOverflowException and denial of service.
verdicts.why: F05 is about the mutual recursion among the decoding routines with no depth counter: its evidence shows readTable() calling readFieldValue(), which in turn dispatches `case 'F': value = readTable(in);` and `case 'A': value = readArray(in);`, closing the cycle. Nesting depth in the attacker-supplied input controls recursion depth, which is the mechanism D2 describes and the exact thing F05 claims is exploitable (stack overflow DoS).
